items.title: The Duskbloods looks like Elden Ring: Nightreign but it’s something different: an evolution of Sekiro and Bloodborne
items.summary: This past weekend we got to try The Duskbloods, FromSoftware’s new game. Despite some connection problems, inevitable since it was a server test, it w
items.content:
Its matches revolve around PvP, with PvE as setup

This past weekend we got to try The Duskbloods, FromSoftware’s new game. Despite some connection problems, inevitable since it was a server test, it was an experience that let us assess what this new game from one of the most distinctive studios working today has to offer . Because the most interesting thing is that, although FromSoftware has a very particular style, they always bring something different. And this time was no exception, with something that may recall Elden Ring: Nightreign , but owes more to Sekiro and Bloodborne than it seems.

While The Duskbloods is a mix of PvP and PvE, the important part is the former. The whole PvE side is a formality where we have to manage our resources well. It’s the part where we can improve our character, gain a certain advantage (or not), and keep improving our standing . But the game really begins when we have to face our rivals.

Although FromSoftware has insisted that it’s possible to make it all the way to the end of each match without facing any other player, this isn’t exactly true. While it’s possible to do so, it means forming alliances and making sure not to face rivals directly . The game’s system allows our rivals to face each other and, with luck, for us to simply survive while they fight or we all ignore one another, but the whole game pushes toward one outcome: confrontation.

Because the game is divided into different phases, there’s a strict time limit. And at the end of each phase one player will be sacrificed. That means that, whether you like it or not, there’s always a reason to get more points and try to stay in the match . Even someone who doesn’t want to face other players or get involved will soon feel compelled if they fall behind, because that’s The Duskbloods’ big trick: it isn’t necessary to face other players until the end of each match, but the system itself encourages confrontations to happen so you don’t get knocked out of the match.

And it’s precisely in fights against other players where the game shines most. Although against AI-controlled enemies it’s possible to notice some details of the game, like the slightly stiffer movement or the greater emphasis on the game’s verticality, it isn’t until we face other players that it becomes obvious what’s different about this game.

From what we’ve been able to play, The Duskbloods seems subtly different from what we’ve seen in previous FromSoftware games. Especially when it comes to the chances of getting out of difficult situations. Although there are dodges and our character moves and jumps quickly, when we face human rivals with attacks similar to our own, that advantage drops off sharply . Making it practically impossible to rely exclusively on our reflexes: we have to avoid being in the places where they can hit us.

That’s the most interesting thing about The Duskbloods. It doesn’t feel like a parry or a dodge at the right time can get us out of most situations. With large-caliber firearms, enemies as mobile as we are, and far fewer iframes than in previous games, the battle feels harsher . Fairer. And that’s what’s interesting.

Because it seems that this is where FromSoftware’s future may lie. That the next iteration after Bloodborne and Sekiro , a game more focused on action and that strips back the RPG elements, could go in this direction: fully embracing it as a one-on-one fight where what matters is spacing and timing . Something that in The Duskbloods seems like it could happen in some frantic and hugely interesting player-versus-player fights that we’re eager to try in its final version, whenever that may be.

items.title: More players applied for The Duskbloods closed network test than for Elden Ring Nightreign, despite Switch 2 exclusivity
items.summary: The first Closed Network Test was unplayable for most players, before From Software ended it early…
items.content:
The first Closed Network Test was unplayable for most players, before From Software ended it early

Video Game News 25th Aug 2026 / 3:19 pm Posted by Jordan Middler Despite being a Nintendo Switch 2 exclusive, more players applied for The Duskbloods’ closed network test than for Elden Ring Nightreign’s test, From Software has claimed.

According to From Software [313 articles]" href=https://www.videogameschronicle.com/companies/fromsoftware/ >From Software producer Yasuhiro Kitao [33 articles]" href=https://www.videogameschronicle.com/people/yasuhiro-kitao/ >Yasuhiro Kitao during a livestream hosted by Famitsu (translated by GamesRadar+ ), The Duskbloods [21 articles]" href=https://www.videogameschronicle.com/games/the-duskbloods/ >The Duskbloods test has been a huge success in terms of the number of players who applied to be part of it. “We were really surprised,” Kitao said.

The Duskbloods network test was marred by issues , perhaps due to this extreme popularity. The test was due to begin on August 21, however, many players were met with a message reading, “Failed to log in to The Duskbloods game server. Select “OK” to attempt to log in again.”

From Software ended the Network Test session early in response to the errors with a statement on social media , saying, “We sincerely apologize for any inconvenience caused to those who were waiting for the first The Duskbloods network test due to game server issues.

“We regret to inform you that today’s session is now closed. We will continue to work on improving the servers and will announce future schedules at a later date.”

VGC went to Japan to speak to Hidetaka Miyazaki about The Duskbloods and the future of From Software .

“I did come into this not being a big PvP player, that is definitely one element of the discussion,” he told VGC.

“But while my nerves and reaction speeds are shot at this point, there are many other ways I can enjoy The Duskbloods and use the situation to my advantage. I like to sneak around and observe the battlefield and strike while others are fighting, or drop in as a third party and cause havoc, just mess with other players.”

“There are many ways to play The Duskbloods, and the main reason you’re playing this game is not necessarily to engage in PvP, but to win at the end of the day.”

items.title: Despite being a Switch 2 exclusive, The Duskbloods closed network test had more applications than Elden Ring Nightreign, surprising even FromSoftware
items.summary: Perhaps because it may be FromSoftware's most mysterious game yet, The Duskbloods' recent network test has seen a lot of player interest.
items.content:
Image credit: FromSoftware News by Sherif Saed Senior Contributor Published on Aug. 25, 2026, 11:31 a.m. 7 comments Follow Elden Ring: Nightreign The Duskbloods is already looking like it's going to be a very popular game. Developer FromSoftware revealed the game's network test, which finished yesterday , attracted more player applications than those for Elden Ring Nightreign , despite it only being available for one platform: Switch 2 .

Game producer Yasuhiro Kitao revealed the news during a Famitsu livestream (via GamesRadar ), and said the team was surprised to see that response.

As with Nightreign's network test, The Duskbloods' network test required signing up ahead of time . Not all players who signed up were guaranteed an invite, though, so it's impressive many decided to do it for only a chance to play the game early

Of course, compared to Nightreign, The Duskbloods' potential player base is far smaller, as the game is a Switch 2 exclusive. Though Nintendo's hybrid console has been breaking sales records , its installed base is significantly smaller than PS5 and Xbox Series X/S combined, the two platforms Nightreign's test ran on. Nightreign also released on PC, PS4 and Xbox One, making for an even larger potential audience.

That was something Kitao brought up during the livestream, saying that the studio wonders if The Duskbloods will have more day-one players based on player interest in the test, despite the Switch 2's smaller installed base.

The Duskbloods' network test hasn't been without problems, though. Its first session ended abruptly following major connectivity issues . Later sessions seemingly ran more smoothly, however. The Duskbloods still does not have a release date, even if, briefly , it looked like it would be released 24th September .

items.title: The Duskbloods Network Test Surpassed Elden Ring Nightreign in Applicants
items.summary: Despite its exclusivity to the Nintendo Switch 2, the first network test for The Duskbloods drew an impressive turnout.
items.content:
The Duskbloods Network Test Surpassed Elden Ring Nightreign in Applicants From DualShockers (Written by Daniel Trock) on August 25, 2026 | OpenCritic

In this day and age, I guess it really shouldn’t be especially surprising that a new game from FromSoftware is a hot-button topic. Even back when Elden Ring Nightreign was announced and people were skeptical about its pseudo-battle royale multiplayer format, it didn’t stop an outpouring of applicants for the game’s initial test runs last year, nor its success at full launch.

While FromSoft’s pedigree does carry a natural disposition toward success, there were factors against the recent network test for its newest multiplayer endeavor, The Duskbloods , chief among them being its exclusivity to the Nintendo Switch 2.

However, it seems that once again, nothing can stand in FromSoft’s way, because as its staff tells it, not only was the first network test for The Duskbloods a rousing success, it actually managed to draw more applicants than Elden Ring Nightreign did.

Whether or not that’s proof positive that the game will be another slam dunk remains to be seen, but if nothing else, it’s clear that the obstacle of platform exclusivity is no obstacle at all to fans of Soulslikes. Either that, or the initial announcement that The Duskbloods would be Switch 2-exclusive got a lot of people...

items.title: Elden Ring Tarnished Edition – 15 Details To Know Before You Jump In
items.summary: FromSoftware's open-world masterpiece finally comes to Nintendo Switch 2. Here's what you should know, including everything new.
items.content:
A fter being delayed from last year, FromSoftware is finally ready to release Elden Ring Tarnished Edition for the Nintendo Switch 2 on August 28th. Of course, we’re no stranger to the original – it won tons of Game of the Year awards in its launch year (including our own) and sold tens of millions of copies. To say that it was the most impactful release of 2022 would be an understatement, and it will finally be available for Nintendo fans later this month.

So what should you expect from the package, which retails for a whopping $79.99? Let’s dive into everything, starting with…

Includes the Base Game and Shadow of the Erdtree

For this price, you get both the base Elden Ring experience and its expansion, Shadow of the Erdtree . We’ll get into each of their content next, but even if they’re years old, these still represent the best open-world and Souls-like titles out there with tons of replay value.

Your journey will begin in the Lands Between, specifically Limgrave, as you venture to the Legacy Dungeons, defeat their bosses and claim the Great Runes, all in an effort to reforge the Elden Ring . And while things are a bit more complicated than that, especially when it comes to further opening up the world, you don’t have to follow a specific order. Heck, it’s possible to skip certain story bosses and still finish the game.

Shadow of the Erdtree , however, is a different beast entirely. Don’t let the “expansion” moniker fool you – it’s a sizable experience in its own right, set in the Land of Shadow. It’s highly vertical, which is both especially perilous and ripe with secrets, from challenging bosses to clues about the Queen Marika. Featuring some of the toughest bosses in the genre, it also has a separate progression track where collecting Scadutree Fragments can boost damage dealt and taken (which can be completely foregone if you seek more of a challenge).

Combining elements of Breath of the Wild with FromSoftware’s own Dark Souls series, the Lands Between and the Land of Shadow offer unprecedented freedom compared to most other open-world titles. I can’t really say it’s the ideal Souls-like for newcomers, but when you realize that exploration is essentially how you get stronger, every nook and cranny holds wondrous possibilities. Find hidden caves, tackle field bosses, open chests that teleport you to different places, interact with mysterious NPCs who call you maidenless, a giant Runebear that will make life hell – what more could you want?

Of course, beyond earning Runes, which can increase your stats and overall level, you’ll discover a litany of weapons, spells, items, crafting recipes, and more to help on your journey. One of the best parts is the sheer build variety. Whether you’re looking to play a melee warrior who’s focused on super-heavy two-handers, a spellcaster who relies on magic, or even something in between, there are hundreds of choices available (and that’s before getting into armor sets, talismans, consumables, and so on).

Another key element in all this is Spirit Ashes. While summoning has typically been used in past titles to bring in other players or NPCs, Spirit Ashes work differently. Think of them as AI companions that you can whip out at any time (provided you have enough FP) and which have their own playstyles, be it the blissful Spirit Jellyfish who can build up poison to the literal ender of Golden bloodlines, Black Knife Tiche.

It wouldn’t be a FromSoft title without challenging boss fights, and many worthy adversaries await. Without going into spoilers, Elden Ring offers some of the most involved bosses ever created. They may throw you off with their speed and extensive combos, but the spectacle is unmatched, especially in Shadow of the Erdtree . Once again, not every boss is mandatory (and they aren’t all masterclasses in design), but in terms of sheer variety and breadth, the selection remains unmatched.

Fortunately, there’s co-op, and it works pretty much as it does in FromSoftware’s other titles (Nightreign notwithstanding). You’ll need a Furlcalling Finger Remedy, which exposes various summoning signs in the world. Interact with them afterwards, and you can summon up to two other players to join you. If you’re facing a boss, its health scales in response, so keep that in mind. Those looking to play with friends will need to set up a multiplayer password and, upon entering it, follow the same process and interact with their summoning signs to bring them.

While there’s also PvP through Invasions, whether you’re the one invading through the use of the Duelist’s Furled Finger or being invaded by someone else, FromSoftware actually added a dedicated PvP space in a post-launch update. The Colosseum is a first of sorts, offering three arenas where you can engage in 1v1s, 3v3s or a free-for-all with six players. No outside enemies to get involved, and different rules depending on the location (the Caelid Colosseum, for example, is the only one that allows Spirit Ashes).

Going back to the build variety of Elden Ring , the Tarnished Edition adds two new starting classes to mix things up. There’s the Heavy Knight who wields a massive schmitar and has 17 Endurance and 15 Strength while equipped with heavy armor. And on the other end is the Idus Knight who has an interesting stat spread, with Dexterity the highest at 15 (and seemingly wields a Light Greatsword, a weapon type introduced in Shadow of the Erdtree ).

Aside from the two new armor sets and weapons available with the Heavy Knight and Idus Knight, there are others to look forward to in the Tarnished Edition , some from the Dark Souls series. The Lucatiel’s Set/Mirrah’s Set from Dark Souls 2 and 3 returns alongside the beloved Hollowslayer Greatsword. The jury is out on how much the latter has changed for the Lands Between, but it still looks fantastic.

items.title: The Duskbloods isn't just 'Nintendo Bloodborne', it's better than Elden Ring: Nightreign
items.summary: It doesn't deserve the hate it's been getting.
items.content:
The Duskbloods is a solid multiplayer experience and proof FromSoftware can do more than just traditional soulsborne.

FromSoftware’s Nintendo Switch 2 exclusive, The Duskbloods , recently finally invited players to see what it’s all about - and despite some initial technical hiccups, I actually quite enjoyed it.

Before I dive into my thoughts and feelings, I can confidently say that my time with The Duskbloods was more enjoyable than Elden Ring: Nightreign . That’s not to say I don’t like Nightreign , but aside from the odd game with friends, it never gave me much of a reason to stick around.

The Duskbloods felt different however. Once the server issues were mended and players could finally jump into some matches, it was clear this is more than FromSoftware trying to relive its Bloodborne glory days.

You’ll no doubt have seen some of the memes online, but when it came time to select a character, I felt compelled to choose Zork.

This goofy little guy perfectly exemplifies why The Duskbloods is a completely different animal to any other FromSoftware game.

Each character has their own unique design, fighting style, special abilities and general stat loadout. As a strength build aficionado, Zork looked like the right choice for me and boy oh boy was I correct.

Aside from his heavy weapon and bulky armour, Zork’s ability lets him ascend into the air and become a living missile directed at anything you’re locked on to.

I let out a hearty chuckle every time I chased down a fleeing player with this move, and even when I went off course and paid the price, it was still a good laugh. His other move is a missile barrage, which was great for pummelling enemies at range.

Once you’re accustomed to what your character can do, your objective is to kill. Like Elden Ring: Nightreign , slaying enemies gradually levels you up, but what I love about The Duskbloods is there’s no penalty for biting off more than you can chew. If you die, your level remains the same, meaning you can spawn back in and have another go, or wander off in search of easier prey.

Sigils are scattered throughout the map hiding powerful NPC allies, which you can summon like eldritch Pokémon to help you overpower foes, or just draw their attention while you heal up from afar. Again, this gave me a good laugh, especially one that sang opera before giving an unsuspected enemy the prime Hoarah Loux experience (just straight hands and elbow drops).

The ultimate goal is to raise your level as high as possible within the time-limit, as the players with the lowest rank get eliminated from the game.

Those fortunate or skilled enough to make it to the end take part in one final battle against your fellow survivors, for the ultimate glory.

In essence, that’s what I loved most about The Duskbloods, and it completely rid me of my woes over the game being PvPvE.

items.title: It Wasn't Fun To Lose In The Duskbloods Network Test
items.summary: What if someone just irredeemably sucks at PvP?
items.content:
After putting well over a hundred hours into Elden Ring Nightreign , I have been stoked out of my mind for The Duskbloods . Even though I had never engaged in FromSoftware PvP before, the PvE aspects of The Duskbloods really appealed to me, and all the previews suggested that the game itself would include enough of a balance of both that I could get by being somewhat mediocre at murdering other players…at least until the final clash. I braced myself: I was probably going to lose a lot, and that was fine. I was going to have fun!

Well, the network test is over now, and I had…some fun, I guess. I also had a pretty bad time, because I lost. A lot. Like, egregiously. And losing was deeply unfun. And I’m struggling to work out in my head if things will be better in the actual game, or if I’m just doomed to suck at The Duskbloods and should give up and go back to Nightreign .

Now, not all my frustration is loss-related. I actually came out of the weekend with the firm conviction that a Network Test is a terrible environment in which to preview a game. For one, I couldn’t play with my friends. I usually play Nightreign in trios with my partner and a good friend. We know that The Duskbloods is only going to be set up for singles and duos, but we were hoping we’d at least be able to all queue into the same game together and compete with each other. I genuinely have no idea if I’ll be able to do that in the final game or not, though, because that feature was unavailable in the Network Test. We did occasionally manage to get into the same games together by queuing at the exact same time and forming alliances when we could. Those moments where we could team up and work together to collect virtue, defend against other players, and take on bosses were some of the best during all my sessions. But it sucked to not be able to consistently share my experience with my friends, and I hope the main game includes that option.

Additionally, the Network Test only had one map available, and a selection of six characters. It took me a while to click with a character, but by the end I ended up liking Trang Lanh quite a bit when I could pair her with a Kin (an NPC ally) that could tank or distract for me a bit. The test also had what I suspect was a deliberately limited pool of bosses and enemies and events. I don’t know that the main game will have more of the latter (it will have three maps and ten characters to start), but if all those options aren’t expanded, it’s going to get real boring, real fast. After a few hours of play, every match felt painfully similar, which I think made losing repeatedly feel even worse than it would have otherwise.

Comment by u/Jam_beter_then_jelly from discussion in TheDuskbloods

Now look. I’m not a sore loser. I suck at all sorts of games and still have fun with them. And I’m extremely willing to admit that PvP is not my bag. But I guess I just thought I’d stand a little more of a chance than I did. The trailers and previews really made it seem like players who wanted to focus more on PvE could use boss fights and exploration to buff themselves up enough to hold their own when it was time to fight. And I think that might be true, but the problem is I kept getting murdered by other players while trying to do these other activities. Folks just swooped in on me and took me out, again and again, then stole my kill or flame or whatever for themselves. On one hand, preventing me from getting virtue and getting some of your own is a viable strategy, I guess. On the other hand, there’s no real reward for killing other players outside of Ritual Sites and certain Sigils (basically specific goals you might have within a match), so getting demolished repeatedly just felt…bad. One guy even killed me, then immediately teleported to the same place I spawned back at, and killed me again before I could get my head on straight. Why!

Also, you have to get really close to people to form Alliances with them, but if you get close your Kin likes to attack unprompted, which often led people to think I was attacking them, which prompted them to attack me while I was menuing and…yeah.

There are demons playing this game by u/kao24429774 in TheDuskbloods

Also , it seemed like so much comes down to those Ritual Sites, zones players are directed to with goals like claiming stones, defending a pledge, or killing other players, such that the end of every phase 2 and 3 was essentially a PvP free-for-all. If I wanted to instead spend that time taking down a Trespasser boss or something, I could, but I’d be doing it alone because everyone else was busy at war in the chapel or clock tower or something. Usually by this time I was desperate enough to try a Ritual Site, but again, I suck at PvP, so I just died. Again and again. After playing for almost ten hours over the weekend, I didn’t make it to the final Grail fight once. The highest high I felt was the one time I managed to defeat my “sworn enemy,” selected for me by my Sigil before he could kill me…only to prompt him to spend the rest of the match hunting me down and killing me over and over and over again. Exciting stuff.

I do want to be clear that I also liked a lot of elements of The Duskbloods . The movement is super fun: I love the quadruple jumps and holy hell that air dash is sick. I love ripping into enemies as the Senator in his dinosaur form, or unleashing a hell of bullets on distant bosses with Layla. All the visual design elements are incredible, from the characters to the Trespasser bosses to the environment itself. I loved finding little hidden areas on the map, like the underground ruins or the top room of the clock tower. I love (most of) the Kin partners, especially the wolf that tears enemies up and the annoyingly persistent Marlowe (the Baritone, however, needs to shut the hell up). And I really, really want to like the premise here: a FromSoftware action game where multiple people are in the world at once, competing and cooperating in different ways simultaneously. That’s cool to me! I want to participate in that!

So, I feel torn. On one hand, this was just the Network Test! It wasn’t here for me to develop complete feelings on the game; it was here to test the networks and make sure they worked, which ( after the first session ) they largely did, very well. Still, it was a valid preview of (some of) what’s to come, provided to myself and other players presumably in the hopes we would enjoy it and want to buy the game. But I didn’t have much fun, and it’s just so hard to tell how much, if any, the vibe of The Duskbloods will change for me upon release. Apparently,you can still progress the story in the full game even if you lose repeatedly, and if that’s the case I might have a better time because at least I’ll feel I’m accomplishing something with each loss. It’s also possible there will be a character in the final roster that I will really click with. It’s also possible that the final game’s skill-based matchmaking will work in my favor more and put me with folks more on my level, or that the meta will develop in such a way as to encourage players to leave me alone while I explore during the first few phases so I’ll have a bit more of a fighting chance in the later ones. Or maybe I’ll just be able to queue with my friends, so even if I lose, I’ll still have fun running around with people I like. Or as the meta develops, maybe I’ll become more familiar with a strategy that will help me collect virtue while avoiding players. That’s a lot of maybes, though!

And it’s also possible that I just, with time, get good. At the moment, I don’t see any world in which I can close the massive skill gap between myself and folks who have been doing this sort of thing for years, but who knows? It’s just, in order to improve, I have to be motivated to play. Losing in a game like this still has to be at least a little fun, or else people like me drop out over time, the skill ceiling keeps rising, and the game gets super sweaty. Is losing over and over at The Duskbloods fun enough to motivate me to improve? In the Network Test, it was unfortunately not. In the main game, it might be. I’m still going to try The Duskbloods out at launch, but the excitement I felt at the prospect of vampire battle royale going into the weekend has had a lot of blood drained out of it.

items.title: The Duskbloods closed network test had more applicants than Elden Ring Nightreign despite being a Switch 2 exclusive, FromSoftware lead reveals
items.content:
Nightreign being multi-platform didn't give it the edge here

(Image credit: FromSoftware) {alert('Link copied')}).catch(err => {console.error('Failed to copy: ', err)})" data-platform="copy_link" data-action="" class="font-ui-heading py-2 text-sm text-neutral-700 hover:bg-neutral-100 transition-colors no-underline block cursor-pointer border-0 bg-transparent w-full text-left normal-case" aria-label="Copy link" role="menuitem" data-analytics-id="article-social" analytics-label="utility-bar-social-share-copy-link" analytics-name="utility-bar-secondary" data-mrf-recirculation="article-social"> Copy link Facebook X Pinterest Flipboard Email Share this article 1 Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter The Duskbloods might be a Nintendo Switch 2-exclusive game, but one FromSoftware lead says that more fans signed up for its closed network test than they did for the multi-platform Elden Ring Nightreign .

Between Elden Ring Nightreign's release last year and The Duskbloods coming this year, FromSoftware is truly in its multiplayer era right now. It's not that the studio is changing its trajectory to ditch single-player games , mind you, as boss Hidetaka Miyazaki says, "both of those ideas just coincided with being multiplayer games. It's not necessarily some big reveal saying that this is the direction we plan to go moving forward."

Perhaps, though, the success of last year's co-op, roguelike-flavored souls game left more folks excited to see what the studio was cooking up with The Duskbloods. In a livestream hosted by Famitsu (translated by GamesRadar+), FromSoftware producer Yasuhiro Kitao reveals that the number of applications for the Switch 2 game's closed network test exceeded that for Nightreign's. "We were really surprised," he notes.

It is surprising, given that the Switch 2 is a single platform – and one that only just launched last year – it's bound to have a smaller installed base than the combined force of PC, PS5, PS4, Xbox Series X|S, and Xbox One, as Nightreign has. Kitao acknowledges this, saying that FromSoftware questions if there really will be more Duskbloods players come launch, and noting that it'll probably be Nightreign that comes out on top.

Even so, it's a positive early sign for The Duskbloods. After all, multiplayer-focused games live and die by how many players they have – their popularity is usually what makes the difference between something being supported for years to come, or being quietly shelved.

I'm GamesRadar+'s Deputy News Editor, working alongside the rest of the news team to deliver cool gaming stories that we love. After spending more hours than I can count filling The University of Sheffield's student newspaper with Pokemon and indie game content, and picking up a degree in Journalism Studies, I started my career at GAMINGbible where I worked as a journalist for over a year and a half. items.title: Kingdom Hearts Difficulty Is Being Compared To Dark Souls
items.summary: Longtime Kingdom Hearts fans know the struggle well, but the series’ recent comeback has clued in a lot of newcomers.
items.content:
By George Foster Published Aug 23, 2026, 1:19 PM EDT George is the Lead News Editor for TheGamer, and has been working in the industry since 2021 after graduating from the University of South Wales with a bachelor's degree in Journalism. He has also previously written for RPG Site, WhatCulture, and PlayStation Lifestyle. George is an expert on platformers, action games, and fighters, but tends to play as many releases as possible. This hands-on experience lets him dive into gaming communities and follow the latest trends. Some of the games George has extensively covered first-hand include Dead Rising, Dragon Ball: Sparking Zero, Assassin's Creed Shadows, and Ninja Gaiden 4. Sign in to your TheGamer account Add Us Add on Google Preferred Source Google News Summary Generate a summary of this story Like Like follow Follow followed Followed Thread 1 Log in Here is a fact-based summary of the story contents: Try something different: Show me the facts Explain it like I’m 5 Give me a lighthearted recap A viral tweet about the first Kingdom Hearts being “harder than Elden Ring ” has kickstarted a debate about the series’ surprising difficulty.

If you’re a veteran Kingdom Hearts fan like me, then you’re well aware that the series is hiding some truly challenging moments underneath its colourful Disney facade . Dragon Maleficent, Demyx, Lingering Will, Young Xehanort, and Yozora are some of the most notable examples of the series’ toughest boss battles, and there are so many more I could mention .

Don’t even get me started on doing it all on Critical difficulty…

While Kingdom Hearts fans have been getting beaten up by Kurt Ziza for nearly 25 years now, there are plenty of people who don’t know just how hard things can get. The series’ recent resurgence in popularity seems to have made that much clearer, though, and some players are even comparing it to Dark Souls and Elden Ring.

Over the past few months, Kingdom Hearts has risen from its four-year nap and finally brought the series back into the spotlight. That, coupled with a recent Steam sale, has made the series more popular than ever and encouraged a bunch of new players to jump into the wild world of Disney and Final Fantasy for the first time.

It seems that some of those new players are having a tougher time than they expected, with one particularly viral tweet from Twitter user whyc3lty suggesting the first Kingdom Hearts is “harder than Elden Ring”. They’re not alone either, as herapathx called the game “hard as s**t” and coined the wonderful phrase, “Disney Dark Souls”.

Both of those tweets have gone viral over the past few days, suggesting that quite a lot of people are having the same realisation about the first game. The wonderful Kingdom Hearts community has responded with some genuinely helpful tips in a thread by Twitter user ChronoKatie , including using Aero, not picking the Sword, and, most importantly, dodge rolling at all times.

While Kingdom Hearts obviously isn’t as difficult as either Dark Souls or Elden Ring, it is much tougher than a lot of people realise. The first game especially has some very specific mechanics and design that make it a bit of a pain if you don’t know what you’re doing. I just can’t wait to see what those same players think when they eventually go up against any of the infamous superbosses…

items.title: ELDEN RING - RAGING WOLF 1/6 SCALE STATUE
items.summary: Who is the Raging Wolf? Among the first Tarnished to join the Roundtable Hold was Vargram, a warrior of great skill and ferocity. He acquired the title of the Raging Wolf from the white wolf pelt that flowed from his helm. Vargram sought to
items.content:
Who is the Raging Wolf?

Among the first Tarnished to join the Roundtable Hold was Vargram, a warrior of great skill and ferocity. He acquired the title of the Raging Wolf from the white wolf pelt that flowed from his helm. Vargram sought to become the shadow of one of the Empyreans and built his strength relentlessly as he traveled through fallow Limgrave to the golden city of Leyndell. And yet in spite of all his strength, his armor is now worn by another… An unnamed Tarnished now walks the Lands Between in the skin of the wolf. Does this warrior seek the same fate as Vargram, forever stalking at the side of an Empyrean? Will they uphold the Golden Order or supplant it for some new code? Whatever the destination, woe befall upon any who dare block the path.

The most impressive Elden Ring statue yet

Standing at 33 cm/13 inches, it’s one of the largest character statues ever produced for ELDEN RING. Crafted with the attentive supervision of FromSoftware, this full 1/6 scale figure captures each minute detail with masterful skill. The size allows perfect fidelity to the beautiful and dark fantasy atmosphere of the game, including smears of bloody red across blade of the Bastard Sword and the crest of the Iron Roundshield. From the intricate filigrees of its helm to its whisps of silvered fur blown back by an errant breeze to the humble, dusty cloth wraps protecting the feet of its greaves against the mossy stones of the path to Stoneveil Castle, it’s a portrait of the implacable will of the Tarnished. All these expertly rendered touches from sculpturer Shinya Yamaoka make this statue a perfect match to the most iconic set from one of the most iconic games of this generation.

Where can I get a Raging Wolf Set statue?

Pre-orders for the Raging Wolf 1/6 scale statue can be placed on the official Bandai Namco website. At this time, based on the production estimates of Gecco studio, these stunning PVC/ABS figures will ship to your home in Winter of 2026. If you are a true aficionado of the game, there is no better purchase to bring the world of Elden Ring to your home or office. It’s a timeless piece for your own collection or an impressive gift for a friend or loved one. And one small note, if you have not yet found this set in the Lands Between for your Tarnished, we recommend you seek the aid of Recusant Bernahl at the Volcano Manor.

Place your order for the Raging Wolf statue on the official Bandai Namco Store.

*This product is available on the Bandai Namco Store in Europe, Australia, the Middle East, India, and the United States.

items.title: ELDEN RING: SHADOW OF THE ERDTREE – Official Vinyl Soundtrack
items.summary: Follow in the foosteps of Miquella once more with this exclusive 2 disc vinyl collection, celebrating the sweeping, emotional journey of Shadow of the Erdtree. Presented with the reverence merited by a legendary expansion, this premium set
items.content:
Follow in the foosteps of Miquella once more with this exclusive 2 disc vinyl collection, celebrating the sweeping, emotional journey of Shadow of the Erdtree.

Presented with the reverence merited by a legendary expansion, this premium set is crafted for collectors, audiophiles, and Tarnished who seek to experience the Realm of Shadow through its music.

The Collection

Housed in a full color gatefold sleeve and marked with the symbol of Messmer the Impaler, each vinyl disc is pressed on heavyweight material to ensure optimal durability and warmth of playback. Whether displayed proudly on a shelf or played to relive your own quest, this set is designed as both a collector’s piece and a lasting tribute to one of the most celebrated expansions in modern gaming.

The Artists

Across 18 tracks, the soundtrack transforms the ELDEN RING experience into a powerful standalone odyssey—one carried by orchestral grandeur, ethereal choir work, and the signature melancholy that defines the worlds created by FromSoftware.

A Collector’s Treasure

This official vinyl set is an essential centerpiece for any discerning fan’s collection. Perfect for longtime followers of FromSoftware’s musical legacy or newcomers drawn into the Land of Shadow for the first time. *This vinyl is available exclusively on the Bandai Namco Store in Europe, Australia, Middle East, India and the United States

items.title: Discover the ELDEN RING Blaidd The Half-Wolf Lamp
items.summary: Summon the legendary warrior into your world with the Blaidd The Half-Wolf Lamp, a handcrafted, LED-powered tribute to one of ELDEN RING ’s most iconic character. Designed for collectors, lore enthusiasts, and Tarnished alike, this unique n
items.content:
Summon the legendary warrior into your world with the Blaidd The Half-Wolf Lamp, a handcrafted, LED-powered tribute to one of ELDEN RING’s most iconic character.

Designed for collectors, lore enthusiasts, and Tarnished alike, this unique night lamp captures the tragic loyalty and silent strength of Blaidd, Shadow of Ranni.

The lamp features an LED-illuminated base that reveals glowing rune symbols beneath Blaidd’s feet, evoking the grace-given power that guides Tarnished across the Lands Between. Rising above it, an engraved acrylic summoning panel glows softly when lit, capturing the look and feel of an in-game summon sign and the spirit-calling magic it represents. Powered through a simple USB connection, it offers effortless illumination for any desk, gaming setup, or collector’s display.

"If ever thou shouldst call upon me… I shall come."

Blaidd’s oath echoes still. Now, he stands ready, not for battle, but as a silent guardian of your space.

Bring the moonlit magic of ELDEN RING into your world, one glowing rune at a time.

*This edition is available exclusively on the Bandai Namco Store in Europe, Australia and the United States.
